title: Lesion atlas: conotruncal lesions (tetralogy, transposition, DORV, common trunk)

items.question: The four-chamber view is normal. Which views find most outflow tract lesions at screening?
options: Four-chamber view at a different angle
items.explanation: Outflow lesions are found with the outflow, three-vessel and three-vessel-and-trachea views and often show little on the four-chamber view.

items.question: You see a ventricular septal defect with an overriding great vessel. Which list is the differential the guideline gives?
options: Tetralogy of Fallot, pulmonary atresia with VSD, double-outlet right ventricle, common arterial trunk
items.explanation: These four make up the differential of a VSD with an overriding vessel.

items.question: Tetralogy of Fallot: the outflow and duct look patent. Why still image the branch pulmonary arteries at their origins?
options: Discontinuity, segmental stenosis and major aortopulmonary collaterals can coexist with a patent-looking outflow
Because the branches are always absent in tetralogy
Only to measure the heart rate
It is not needed when the outflow looks patent
items.explanation: The branch pulmonary arteries must be identified at their origins for exactly this reason.

items.question: Tetralogy of Fallot. Why image the arch and the thymus?
options: To tailor counselling to the risk of 22q11 deletion
items.explanation: Imaging the arch and the thymus allows counselling tailored to the risk of 22q11 deletion.

items.question: Absent pulmonary valve syndrome. Which pair of findings fits?
options: Hypoplastic annulus with to-and-fro flow; dilated main and branch pulmonary arteries
Large annulus with forward flow only; small pulmonary arteries
Absent tricuspid valve; small right ventricle
items.explanation: APVS shows a hypoplastic annulus with tiny leaflets and to-and-fro flow, and dilated main and branch pulmonary arteries with an enlarged right heart.

items.question: Tetralogy with absent pulmonary valve. Why does the side of the aortic arch matter?
options: An aneurysmal branch pulmonary artery on the same side may compress the airway
It decides the mode of delivery
It does not matter in this lesion
items.explanation: Arch position matters because an aneurysmal ipsilateral branch pulmonary artery may compress the airway.

items.question: Double-outlet right ventricle with a subpulmonary defect. What else must be imaged carefully, and why?
options: The aortic arch, because subaortic obstruction and coarctation often accompany it
The ductus venosus, because it is often absent
The pulmonary veins, because they are always anomalous
Nothing else; the defect is the whole lesion
items.explanation: The anterior aorta may be obstructed below the valve and coarctation often accompanies it, so the arch needs careful 2D and colour imaging.

items.question: Common arterial trunk with a right aortic arch. What is the stated risk of 22q11 deletion?
options: Exactly the same as with a left arch
items.explanation: In common arterial trunk a right aortic arch is associated with a 22q11 deletion risk above 50%.

items.question: Common arterial trunk. Which valve finding can affect survival before birth?
options: None; the trunk is well tolerated in every case
items.explanation: Truncal valve function, especially significant regurgitation, can affect survival in utero.

items.question: D-transposition is diagnosed at 22 weeks. What must be assessed late in gestation?
items.explanation: Every fetus with D-transposition should have the foramen ovale assessed late in gestation, with delivery where the atrial communication can be enlarged.

items.question: A posterior pulmonary artery arises from the left ventricular outflow. Does this alone tell you it is D-transposition?
options: No: corrected transposition shows the same appearance
Yes: it only occurs in D-transposition
Yes, if the heart rate is normal
No: it is a normal variant
items.explanation: Both D-transposition and congenitally corrected transposition show a posterior pulmonary artery from the left ventricular outflow.

items.question: Congenitally corrected transposition. Which rhythm problem must serial studies watch for?
items.explanation: Rhythm abnormalities including congenital heart block can arise in fetal life; serial studies should be offered.
